nameStory: Ragged-robin gets its wonderfully descriptive name from its distinctive flowers that look like they've been through a shredder! Each pink petal is deeply cut into four narrow strips, giving the bloom a delightfully tattered, ragged appearance that's impossible to mistake once you've seen it.
description: Ragged-robin is a charming perennial wildflower that stands 1-3 feet tall with an upright, branching habit. Originally from Europe and Asia, this member of the pink family has naturalized in parts of New England, particularly in wet meadows and marshes. Its most striking feature is its unique pink flowers with deeply divided, ribbon-like petals that create an almost feathery appearance from late spring through summer.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Bright pink flowers with five petals, each deeply cut into four narrow strips that look ragged or fringed. The flowers are about an inch across and clustered at the top of stems, with a sweet, subtle fragrance.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Narrow, lance-shaped leaves arranged in opposite pairs along the stem. The leaves feel smooth and slightly waxy to the touch, with prominent parallel veins running lengthwise.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Grows in loose clumps 1-3 feet tall with multiple branching stems. The plant has a somewhat sprawling nature, especially in rich, moist soils where it can lean on neighboring vegetation.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Produces small, egg-shaped capsules that split open at the top when ripe, releasing tiny dark seeds. The capsules often persist into fall, giving a rattling sound when shaken.

habitat: In New England, ragged-robin thrives in consistently moist to wet areas like marshes, wet meadows, stream edges, and boggy ground. It prefers full sun to partial shade and rich, organic soils that stay damp throughout the growing season. You're most likely to find it in areas that flood seasonally or have a high water table.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges as rosettes of narrow leaves in early spring. The plant begins sending up flowering stems by late spring, with buds forming at the stem tips.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming occurs from late May through August, with the distinctive ragged pink flowers most abundant in early to mid-summer. The sweet fragrance is strongest on warm, humid mornings.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade and seed capsules mature, turning brown and splitting open. The foliage may yellow but often stays green well into fall in wet locations.
seasonality.winter: Above-ground parts die back completely, leaving only the root system alive underground. Look for dried stems and seed capsules persisting through early winter.

funFact: Ragged-robin flowers are specially designed for long-tongued visitors - their nectar is stored so deep in the flower tube that only butterflies and long-tongued bees can reach it, while the ragged petals serve as perfect landing platforms for these pollinators!
confusionNotes: The deeply cut, ragged petals make this flower nearly impossible to confuse with anything else in New England. Other pink wildflowers in wet areas have whole, uncut petals, making ragged-robin's shredded appearance a dead giveaway.
contextualKnowledge: Though ragged-robin is not native to North America, it has been cultivated in gardens for centuries and occasionally escapes to suitable wild habitats. In its native Europe, it's considered an indicator species of high-quality wet meadows and is valued in wildlife gardening for supporting butterflies and other pollinators.
compareHints: Among its catchfly relatives, ragged-robin is unique for its deeply divided petals - other Silene species like white campion and bladder campion have whole, uncut petals. While fire pink shares the bright color, its petals are pointed but not ragged, and red campion has rounded, whole petals rather than the distinctive shredded appearance of ragged-robin.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among its catchfly relatives, white campion stands out for being densely fuzzy all over, while most other Silene species are smoother.
Among the catchflies and campions in New England, bladder campion is the only one with those distinctive inflated, balloon-like sepals - this feature alone separates it from all its relatives.
Among its catchfly relatives, rose campion is unmistakable due to its completely silver-woolly appearance and intense magenta flowers.
Red campion stands out from its Silene relatives by its bright pink color and preference for disturbed, rich soils.
Among its catchfly relatives, wild pink is distinguished by its extremely low, mat-forming growth habit and spring blooming time.
Among its catchfly relatives, sleepy catchfly stands out for having the smallest, least showy flowers that barely open.
Unlike its catchfly relatives that often have white or pale pink flowers, Maltese-cross blazes with intense scarlet-red blooms.
Unlike its taller relatives like white campion or bladder campion that grow as upright herbs in lower elevations, moss campion has evolved this unique cushion form specifically for alpine survival.
Among the catchflies and campions, starry campion stands out with its deeply fringed star-like petals and whorled leaf arrangement.
Among the red-flowered catchflies, royal catchfly stands out for its impressive height and late summer bloom time.
Among its catchfly relatives, night-flowering catchfly is unique for its extremely sticky, clammy texture and strict evening-flowering schedule.
Fire pink stands out dramatically from its catchfly relatives by its intense red color - most other Silene species have white, pink, or pale flowers.
Unlike white campion and bladder campion which have white flowers, sand catchfly's bright pink petals make it stand out.
Balkan catchfly is much smaller and more delicate than the common bladder campion, which has inflated balloon-like calyxes behind its flowers.
